tips.li: Fruit and vegetables count raw or cooked into meals. Survival meals, pemmican, kibble and meat alone don't.
A simple meal made with vegetables keeps scurvy away as well as a fine one does. Set the stove's ingredients to include them.
Berries from the wild count. A few days' foraging in summer can carry a colony through a stretch of preserved food.
[!lowtech] A hydroponics basin grows vegetables all winter, out of the cold and out of reach of blight.
Friendships grow from shared work and shared meals. Put them on the same job as someone who likes them a little already.
A party or a calendar day brings everyone together, and the quiet ones talk more at a gathering than anywhere else.
Someone with no friend here is likelier to break, and feels left out when the others' circles close.
Tension with a camp grows as they hunt and cut wood on the colony's land, faster when they break the terms the council set.
A gift eases tension, and is remembered when they leave.
A camp that boils over turns on the colony. Settle a quarrel early, or ask them to move on before it comes to that.
A feast day goes best with food in store and a free evening. A day of games needs a quiet day with no raid on the map.
A day kept three years running becomes a tradition, and letting a tradition pass disappoints everyone.
Days the colony doesn't want to keep can be let pass, renamed or kept another way from the Calendar page.
Graves inside the home area get cleaned with everything else. Outside it, nobody tends them.
A small fenced graveyard with a few flowers is somewhere to grieve, and the remembrance walk goes there each spring once it's a custom.
Graves somewhere tidy and close give the calendar's days of remembrance somewhere to go.
Clothes under half their condition give a bad mood. A tailor's bench and some cloth or leather fixes it for good.
Clothes taken from the dead give most people a bad mood. Keep them for selling, not for wearing.
An outfit policy that only allows clothes above half condition makes colonists change out of rags by themselves.
Two hours of recreation in the evening is usually enough. Colonists with no recreation hours only rest when they're desperate.
"Anything" hours count too: colonists fill them with recreation when they need it.
A hard-working colony can still keep an hour or two of recreation. It loses less to mental breaks than it gains from the extra work.
Strain drains with quiet days, good sleep, recreation, friends and gatherings. A rest day from the calendar or a decree helps everyone at once.
A strained colonist can still look cheerful. Their mood tab shows how close they are to breaking under the surface.
Grief, fear and dread add strain every hour they last. Ease the cause and the strain follows.
Rest in bed shortens convalescence by about a third. Working while still weak can set it back.
A medical bed in a clean room keeps a convalescent resting; a visit from a friend makes it easier to bear.
Light work is better than heavy: hauling and cleaning tire them less than mining or building.
A promise buys a wish more time and keeps the trust it would lose, as long as the promise is kept.
Some wishes are cheap to grant and dear to ignore: a meal, a day off, a word from the council.
Letting a wish lapse on purpose is sometimes right. It costs less trust than a promise broken.
